83FAC330DFE601311D1368A86D17958E.description: identify how works of art reflect the environment in which they are created.

83FA6190DFE601311D1268A86D17958E.description: explore vocational and avocational opportunities in the Arts.

83FA0E10DFE601311D1168A86D17958E.description: utilize interrelated elements among the Arts and other subject areas.

83F9CD30DFE601311D1068A86D17958E.description: compare and explain how the characteristic materials of each art (e.g., sound in music, visual stimuli in visual arts, movement in dance, human interrelationships in theatre) correlate to similar events, scenes, emotions, or ideas.

83F98C40DFE601311D0F68A86D17958E.description: Students make connections among the Arts, other subject areas, life, and work.

83F94B40DFE601311D0E68A86D17958E.description: determine the connection of a work of art to societal and cultural change or preservation, including American Indian culture and art.

83F90810DFE601311D0D68A86D17958E.description: demonstrate appropriate audience behavior for the context and style of art presented.

83F8BA60DFE601311D0C68A86D17958E.description: describe how people's emotions and experiences influence the development of specific art works.

83F87890DFE601311D0B68A86D17958E.description: compare various reasons for creating works of art.

83F83550DFE601311D0A68A86D17958E.description: identify, describe, and analyze specific works of art as belonging to particular cultures, times and places in the context in which they were created.

83F7E6D0DFE601311D0968A86D17958E.description: demonstrate how history/culture and the Arts influence each other.

83F7A100DFE601311D0868A86D17958E.description: Students understand the role of the Arts in society, diverse cultures, and historical periods.

83F75E60DFE601311D0768A86D17958E.description: describe and compare a variety of individual responses to works of art.

83F71090DFE601311D0668A86D17958E.description: develop and apply criteria for evaluating quality and effectiveness of the work of art.

83F6C5D0DFE601311D0568A86D17958E.description: describe the influence of personal experience on the interpretation of works of art.

83F681C0DFE601311D0468A86D17958E.description: evaluate the quality and effectiveness of their own and other art works by applying specific criteria appropriate to the style and offer constructive suggestions for improvement.

83F63BA0DFE601311D0368A86D17958E.description: Students analyze characteristics and merits of their work and the work of others.

83F5F5F0DFE601311D0268A86D17958E.description: examine the breadth and depth of possible responses presented by media and media techniques.

83F5AFE0DFE601311D0168A86D17958E.description: understand and apply stage direction and ground plans.

83F562E0DFE601311D0068A86D17958E.description: identify and define standard notation symbols including pitch, rhythm, dynamics, tempo, articulation, and expression.

83F4F490DFE601311CFF68A86D17958E.description: use dance elements (space, time, energy) to discuss movement and produce movements demonstrated and/or described in words.

83F2A560DFE601311CF768A86D17958E.description: communicate intended meaning based on their own ideas and concepts from other sources.

83F247A0DFE601311CF668A86D17958E.description: use art materials, techniques, technologies, and processes to create specific responses.

83F47380DFE601311CFD68A86D17958E.description: experiment and practice with a variety of media to achieve clarity of expression.

83F43230DFE601311CFC68A86D17958E.description: use scenery, properties, sound, costume, and make-up to communicate locale and mood.

83F3EEB0DFE601311CFB68A86D17958E.description: use accepted performance and expressive techniques (e.g., breath control, posture) while singing and playing music in small and large ensembles.

83F3A630DFE601311CFA68A86D17958E.description: perform movements and rhythm patterns with control and expression.

83F1DFA0DFE601311CF568A86D17958E.description: Students develop and refine arts skills and techniques to express ideas, pose and solve problems, and discover meaning.

83F19010DFE601311CF468A86D17958E.description: rehearse, perform, and critique storytelling and improvisation.

83F14DE0DFE601311CF368A86D17958E.description: rehearse, perform, and critique musical performances.

83F0C5F0DFE601311CF168A86D17958E.description: exhibit craftsmanship, completion, and develop a body of work.

83F032A0DFE601311CEF68A86D17958E.description: demonstrate examples of historical, contemporary, and traditional visual arts, including American Indian art.

83EFE4C0DFE601311CEE68A86D17958E.description: perform examples of theatre (e.g., comedy, melodrama, plays from historical periods).

83EFA3B0DFE601311CED68A86D17958E.description: perform examples of music (e.g., folk, jazz, ethnic, popular, classical, time period).

83EF5F30DFE601311CEC68A86D17958E.description: identify examples of folk, popular, historical, and contemporary (e.g., ballet, jazz, modern, tap) dance.

83EED880DFE601311CEA68A86D17958E.description: demonstrate and compare examples of cultural, political, communication, expressive, commercial, and environmental visual arts.

83EE9310DFE601311CE968A86D17958E.description: perform examples of music (e.g., ceremonial, celebration, concerts, theatre, dance, film, social, community, entertainment).

83EE3940DFE601311CE868A86D17958E.description: perform in classroom or school programs/productions.

83EDECC0DFE601311CE768A86D17958E.description: identify examples of social, theatrical, and traditional dance.

83ED5C40DFE601311CE568A86D17958E.description: select a course of action using two-dimensional processes (e.g., painting, drawing, printmaking, photography, computer arts) and the three-dimensional processes (e.g., sculpture, indigenous/traditional arts).

83ED1AA0DFE601311CE468A86D17958E.description: perform solo and in ensemble (e.g., mime, live, film, video productions).

83ECD170DFE601311CE368A86D17958E.description: perform vocal and/or instrumental solos, or in ensembles.

83EC71A0DFE601311CE268A86D17958E.description: demonstrate the human body in motion.

83EBDFC0DFE601311CE068A86D17958E.description: apply knowledge of techniques to create works (e.g., painting, drawing, printmaking, photography, computer arts, graphic design, sculpture, and indigenous/traditional arts).

83EB9CA0DFE601311CDF68A86D17958E.description: apply techniques to write, direct, act, and design.

83EB5780DFE601311CDE68A86D17958E.description: apply the techniques of expressive devices, dynamics, tempo, phrasing, accompaniment, interpretation, and improvisation.

83EB0970DFE601311CDD68A86D17958E.description: apply the techniques of body awareness (e.g., control, flexibility, dynamics, expression, musicality) in class and performance.

83EA7DB0DFE601311CDB68A86D17958E.description: apply the elements of plot, character, setting and mood.

83EA3E20DFE601311CDA68A86D17958E.description: apply the elements of space (shape, level, path in space, pattern, form), time (duration, rhythm), and energy (movement quality) to compose dances.

83E9FCA0DFE601311CD968A86D17958E.description: apply the elements of line, shape, form, color, space, value, and texture to compose works of art and the principals of design-pattern, balance, contrast, rhythm, proportion, economy, movement, dominance.

83E9BD80DFE601311CD868A86D17958E.description: apply the elements of rhythm, melody, harmony, timbre/tone color, and form.

83E93570DFE601311CD668A86D17958E.description: Students apply and describe the concepts, structures, and processes in the Arts.

83E8E890DFE601311CD568A86D17958E.description: describe and analyze artistic choices in their own work and works of others.

83E8A230DFE601311CD468A86D17958E.description: collaborate with others to make artistic choices.

83E859C0DFE601311CD368A86D17958E.description: prepare and/or revise works for presentation.

83E80F10DFE601311CD268A86D17958E.description: select a variety of materials and sources to demonstrate a specific art form.

83E7C370DFE601311CD168A86D17958E.description: create a work from their own ideas and images based on themes, symbols, events and personal experiences.

83E77390DFE601311CD068A86D17958E.description: Students create, perform/exhibit, and respond in the Arts.

document.title: Montana Essential Learning Expectations (ELE) for Science

821E09D0DFE601311A1468A86D17958E.description: Identify the impact of science changing human understanding of the natural world on past and present societies.

821DB230DFE601311A1368A86D17958E.description: Identify and discuss examples of science changing human understanding of the natural world

821D58C0DFE601311A1268A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate how humans use their senses to learn about the natural world

821CA0B0DFE601311A1068A86D17958E.description: Describe and explain science as a human endeavor and an ongoing process

821C5690DFE601311A0F68A86D17958E.description: Discuss how milestones have impacted society over time.

821C0740DFE601311A0E68A86D17958E.description: Chart the history of scientific milestones (see Grades 6-8.)

821BB240DFE601311A0D68A86D17958E.description: Identify major milestones in science that have impacted science, technology, and society

821B5310DFE601311A0C68A86D17958E.description: Discuss how technology advances science understanding

821ADF80DFE601311A0B68A86D17958E.description: Identify and discuss scientific discoveries influenced by these technologies

821A7290DFE601311A0A68A86D17958E.description: Identify examples of technological advances throughout history, including Montana American Indian examples

821A2770DFE601311A0968A86D17958E.description: Give examples of scientific discoveries and describe the interrelationship between technological advances and scientific understanding, including Montana American Indian examples

8219C790DFE601311A0868A86D17958E.description: Students understand historical developments in science and technology.

82197790DFE601311A0768A86D17958E.description: Explain the impact of science and technology on Montana American Indians.

82192C70DFE601311A0668A86D17958E.description: Investigate how science and technology have an impact on Montana American Indians

8218E0C0DFE601311A0568A86D17958E.description: Describe how the knowledge of science and technology influences the development of the Montana American Indian cultures

8217CD10DFE601311A0268A86D17958E.description: Identify a local issue with an environmental impact

82177440DFE601311A0168A86D17958E.description: Use scientific knowledge to investigate problems and their proposed solutions and evaluate those solutions while considering environmental impacts

821727F0DFE601311A0068A86D17958E.description: Simulate collaborative problem solving and give examples of how scientific knowledge and technology are shared with other scientists and the public

8216DB40DFE6013119FF68A86D17958E.description: Research and summarize the scientific issues relevant to that local current event or problem

82168C50DFE6013119FE68A86D17958E.description: Identify a local current event or problem involving science

82163A10DFE6013119FD68A86D17958E.description: Apply scientific knowledge and process skills to understand issues and everyday events

8215F290DFE6013119FC68A86D17958E.description: Identify uses of technology unique to specific occupations within each field of science

8215ACE0DFE6013119FB68A86D17958E.description: Identify occupations within specific fields of science

82151C00DFE6013119F968A86D17958E.description: Describe the specific fields of science and technology as they relate to occupations within those fields

8214D060DFE6013119F868A86D17958E.description: Students, through the inquiry process, understand how scientific knowledge and technological developments impact communities, cultures and societies.

821475D0DFE6013119F768A86D17958E.description: Identify scientific theories about the origin and evolution of the earth and solar system

82142BE0DFE6013119F668A86D17958E.description: Identify phases of the moon by how much of the lighted part of moon can be seen from Earth

8213DDD0DFE6013119F568A86D17958E.description: Model the relative movements of the moon, Earth and sun

82138370DFE6013119F468A86D17958E.description: Recognize that the moon is lighted by the sun

82132F50DFE6013119F368A86D17958E.description: Identify the relationship between the Earth, the sun, and the moon

8212D4F0DFE6013119F268A86D17958E.description: Describe the earth, moon, planets and other objects in space in terms of size, force of gravity, structure, and movement in relation to the sun

82127860DFE6013119F168A86D17958E.description: Describe and model the causes of seasons and year due to the revolution and tilt of the Earth in relation to the sun

82121AF0DFE6013119F068A86D17958E.description: Illustrate and model Earth's revolution in relation to the sun

8211C670DFE6013119EF68A86D17958E.description: Explain how the Earth's rotation causes day and night

82117D90DFE6013119EE68A86D17958E.description: Illustrate/model Earth's rotation in relation to the sun

82112F30DFE6013119ED68A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast revolution and rotation

8210D850DFE6013119EC68A86D17958E.description: Describe and model the motion and tilt of earth in relation to the sun, and explain the concepts of day, night, seasons, year, and climatic changes

82108C10DFE6013119EB68A86D17958E.description: Interpret a weather map using correct symbols.

82104040DFE6013119EA68A86D17958E.description: Discuss how interactions of air masses are used to forecast the weather

820FF500DFE6013119E968A86D17958E.description: Describe properties of air masses moving across the earth's surface

820FA800DFE6013119E868A86D17958E.description: Identify different types of clouds and how they can be used to predict weather.

820F57A0DFE6013119E768A86D17958E.description: Explain the water cycle and its application to weather.

820EFE10DFE6013119E668A86D17958E.description: Describe the water cycle, the composition and structure of the atmosphere and the impact of oceans on large-scale weather patterns

820EAE80DFE6013119E568A86D17958E.description: Describe how the relative age of fossils can be determined from their position in sedimentary rock layers

820E53C0DFE6013119E468A86D17958E.description: Recognize that sedimentary rock layers represent a progression of time

820DFD50DFE6013119E368A86D17958E.description: Use fossils to describe the geological timeline

820DA9C0DFE6013119E268A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the differences between rocks and minerals.

820D5990DFE6013119E168A86D17958E.description: Define minerals as the building blocks of rocks.

820CFB20DFE6013119E068A86D17958E.description: Recognize that rock is composed of different kinds of minerals

820C80E0DFE6013119DF68A86D17958E.description: Differentiate between igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks.

820C2C70DFE6013119DE68A86D17958E.description: Differentiate between rocks types and minerals types and classify both by how they are formed and the utilization by humans

820BE330DFE6013119DD68A86D17958E.description: Define the role that plate tectonics play in changing Earth's features

820B9060DFE6013119DC68A86D17958E.description: Explain glaciations and weathering effects on the Earth's surface

820AE340DFE6013119DA68A86D17958E.description: Model and explain the internal structure of the earth and describe the formation and composition of earth's external features in terms of the rock cycle and plate tectonics and constructive and destructive forces

820A93A0DFE6013119D968A86D17958E.description: Students, through the inquiry process, demonstrate knowledge of the composition, structures, processes and interactions of Earth's systems and other objects in space.

820A37A0DFE6013119D868A86D17958E.description: Classify plants by flowering, non-flowering, mosses, ferns

8209E4C0DFE6013119D768A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast two characteristics of the animal kingdoms.

820939C0DFE6013119D568A86D17958E.description: Know the difference between kingdom, phylum and class

82089200DFE6013119D368A86D17958E.description: Employ dichotomous key to separate a collection of basic objects

82084500DFE6013119D268A86D17958E.description: Create and use a basic classification scheme to identify plants and animals

8207F490DFE6013119D168A86D17958E.description: Describe the interdependence between the parts of an ecosystem

82079BB0DFE6013119D068A86D17958E.description: Identify the key characteristics of an ecosystem

8206A220DFE6013119CD68A86D17958E.description: Investigate and explain the interdependent nature of populations and communities in the environment and describe how species in these populations adapt by evolving

82065430DFE6013119CC68A86D17958E.description: Communicate the differences in the reproductive processes of a variety of plants and animals using the principles of genetic modeling (e.g., Punnet squares)

82060310DFE6013119CB68A86D17958E.description: Explain the relationship between photosynthesis and transpiration

8205B750DFE6013119CA68A86D17958E.description: Explain the process of photosynthesis and transpiration in terms of the key structures and compounds that are utlized.

82056B50DFE6013119C968A86D17958E.description: Identify the compounds involved in photosynthesis and transpiration

82051C40DFE6013119C868A86D17958E.description: Identify plant structures involved in photosynthesis and transpiration

8204CD90DFE6013119C768A86D17958E.description: Explain how organisms and systems of organisms obtain and use energy resources to maintain stable conditions (e.g., food webs, photosynthesis, respiration)

82047B40DFE6013119C668A86D17958E.description: Create model/diagram of an animal and/or plant cells.

820374C0DFE6013119C368A86D17958E.description: Describe the basic structure and function of a cell.

82032BC0DFE6013119C268A86D17958E.description: Compare the structure and function of prokaryotic cells (bacteria) and eukaryotic cells (plant, animal, etc.) including the levels of organization of the structure and function, particularly with humans

8202DDD0DFE6013119C168A86D17958E.description: Students, through the inquiry process, demonstrate knowledge of characteristics, structures and function of living things, the process and diversity of life, and how living organisms interact with each other and their environment.

82028D20DFE6013119C068A86D17958E.description: Give examples and describe how energy is transferred and conserved (e.g. electric to light and heat [light bulb], chemical to mechanical [fuel to propulsion])

820236A0DFE6013119BF68A86D17958E.description: Identify, build, describe, measure, and analyze mechanical systems (e.g., simple and complex compound machines) and describe the forces acting within those systems

82019EF0DFE6013119BD68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that work is movement following application of a force.

82014C00DFE6013119BC68A86D17958E.description: Explain the differences between kinetic and potential energy

820101B0DFE6013119BB68A86D17958E.description: Experiment with potential and kinetic energy, (i.e., cars/balls on ramp)

8200B6D0DFE6013119BA68A86D17958E.description: Describe and explain the motion of an object in terms of its position, direction, & speed as well as the forces acting upon it

82005DD0DFE6013119B968A86D17958E.description: Model and explain that states of matter are dependent upon the quantity of energy present in the system and describe what will change and what will remain unchanged at the particulate level when matter experiences an external force or energy change

82001530DFE6013119B868A86D17958E.description: Explain the three types of heat transfer

81FFCE10DFE6013119B768A86D17958E.description: Explain the flow of energy in a circuit.

81FF33D0DFE6013119B568A86D17958E.description: Distinguish the differences between simple, series, and parallel circuits

81FED890DFE6013119B468A86D17958E.description: Define electricity as the flow of energy

81FE7570DFE6013119B368A86D17958E.description: Design and construct instruments that produce sound (The effects of mechanical waves are applied in Standard 4 Benchmark 1)

81FE2E40DFE6013119B268A86D17958E.description: Investigate how sound can be changed.

81FDE6C0DFE6013119B168A86D17958E.description: Explore how sound is produced, transmitted, and received.

81FD9E20DFE6013119B068A86D17958E.description: Describe the processes of sublimation, condensation, and evaporation

81FD5290DFE6013119AF68A86D17958E.description: Identify that most matter can exist as a solid, liquid or gas depending on temperature.

81FD02D0DFE6013119AE68A86D17958E.description: Describe energy and compare and contrast the energy transformations and the characteristics of light, heat, motion, magnetism, electricity, sound and mechanical waves

81FCA9F0DFE6013119AD68A86D17958E.description: Identify examples of chemical change (generating a gas, color change, rust)

81FC50E0DFE6013119AC68A86D17958E.description: Define chemical properties as properties that do change the chemical nature of matter (i.e., combustion, rust, decompose)

81FBFCB0DFE6013119AB68A86D17958E.description: Define physical properties as properties that do not change the chemical nature of matter (i.e., color, smell, freezing point, boiling point, melting point, magnetism)

81FBA790DFE6013119AA68A86D17958E.description: Examine, describe, compare and classify objects and substances based on common physical properties and simple chemical properties

81FB3A00DFE6013119A968A86D17958E.description: Explain the relationship between elements, compounds, pure substances, and mixtures.

81FAC9E0DFE6013119A868A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between pure substances and mixtures

81FA8040DFE6013119A768A86D17958E.description: Identify common compounds (water, carbon dioxide, salt)

81F99F30DFE6013119A468A86D17958E.description: Classify, describe, and manipulate the physical models of matter in terms of: elements, and compounds, pure substances and mixtures, atoms, and molecules

81F950B0DFE6013119A368A86D17958E.description: Students, through the inquiry process, demonstrate knowledge of properties, forms, changes and interactions of physical and chemical systems.

81F8F920DFE6013119A268A86D17958E.description: Explain how Montana American Indians have used observation to explain processes of nature

81F8B190DFE6013119A168A86D17958E.description: Identify examples of Montana American Indians using observation to create knowledge of nature

81F86700DFE6013119A068A86D17958E.description: Compare how observations of nature form an essential base of knowledge among the Montana American Indians.

81F81B00DFE60131199F68A86D17958E.description: Identify strengths and weakness in an investigation design.

81F7CDA0DFE60131199E68A86D17958E.description: Follow step-by-step directions to build a model

81F773F0DFE60131199D68A86D17958E.description: List various types of models including 2-D, 3-D and computer simulations

81F715C0DFE60131199C68A86D17958E.description: Explain the purpose of a model

81F6BD00DFE60131199B68A86D17958E.description: Create models to illustrate scientific concepts and use the model to predict change. (e.g., computer simulation, stream table, graphic representation)

81F67050DFE60131199A68A86D17958E.description: Communicate findings in written or oral format.

81F60E50DFE60131199968A86D17958E.description: Determine if hypothesis is supported or not supported with guidance

81F59890DFE60131199868A86D17958E.description: Compare data to hypothesis with guidance

81F54A10DFE60131199768A86D17958E.description: Review, communicate and defend results of investigations, including considering alternative explanations.

81F47200DFE60131199468A86D17958E.description: Collect data using observation and tools such as scale, balances, thermometer, beaker, digital probes, stop watch, graduated cylinder in metric units

81F42890DFE60131199368A86D17958E.description: Select and use appropriate tools including technology to make measurements (in metric units), gather, process and analyze data from scientific investigations

81F38830DFE60131199168A86D17958E.description: List and follow appropriate safety procedures.

81F33970DFE60131199068A86D17958E.description: Identify a control group and explain its purpose

81F2EEE0DFE60131198F68A86D17958E.description: Identify the independent and dependent variable

81F29B00DFE60131198E68A86D17958E.description: Plan an investigation to test a hypothesis

81F242D0DFE60131198D68A86D17958E.description: Explain the relationship between a testable question and a hypothesis

81F1A520DFE60131198B68A86D17958E.description: Write a testable question for an investigation

81F15740DFE60131198A68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and select a testable question when presented with multiple choices

81F10710DFE60131198968A86D17958E.description: Identify a question, determine relevant variable and a control, formulate a testable hypothesis, plan and predict the outcome of an investigation, safely conduct scientific investigation, and compare and analyze data

81F0AC90DFE60131198868A86D17958E.description: Students, through the inquiry process, demonstrate the ability to design, conduct, evaluate, and communicate results and reasonable conclusions of scientific investigations.

document.title: Montana K-12 Science Content Standards Framework

839E4440DFE601311C6168A86D17958E.description: describe and explain science as a human endeavor and an ongoing process

839E0370DFE601311C6068A86D17958E.description: identify major milestones in science that have impacted science, technology, and society

839DBFF0DFE601311C5F68A86D17958E.description: give examples of scientific discoveries and describe the interrelationship between technological advances and scientific understanding, including Montana American Indian examples

839D7840DFE601311C5E68A86D17958E.description: Students understand historical developments in science and technology.

839D2BC0DFE601311C5D68A86D17958E.description: describe how the knowledge of science and technology influences the development of the Montana American Indian cultures

839CED20DFE601311C5C68A86D17958E.description: use scientific knowledge to investigate problems and their proposed solutions and evaluate those solutions while considering environmental impacts

839CA760DFE601311C5B68A86D17958E.description: simulate collaborative problem solving and give examples of how scientific knowledge and technology are shared with other scientists and the public

839C6080DFE601311C5A68A86D17958E.description: apply scientific knowledge and process skills to understand issues and everyday events

839C1630DFE601311C5968A86D17958E.description: describe the specific fields of science and technology as they relate to occupations within those fields

839BB320DFE601311C5868A86D17958E.description: Students, through the inquiry process, understand how scientific knowledge and technological developments impact communities, cultures and societies.

839B4F30DFE601311C5768A86D17958E.description: identify scientific theories about the origin and evolution of the earth and solar system

839B0CF0DFE601311C5668A86D17958E.description: describe the earth, moon, planets and other objects in space in terms of size, force of gravity, structure, and movement in relation to the sun

839ACAF0DFE601311C5568A86D17958E.description: describe and model the motion and tilt of earth in relation to the sun, and explain the concepts of day, night, seasons, year, and climatic changes

839A88F0DFE601311C5468A86D17958E.description: describe the water cycle, the composition and structure of the atmosphere and the impact of oceans on large-scale weather patterns

839A4640DFE601311C5368A86D17958E.description: use fossils to describe the geological timeline

839A0080DFE601311C5268A86D17958E.description: differentiate between rocks types and minerals types and classify both by how they are formed and the utilization by humans

8399B4C0DFE601311C5168A86D17958E.description: model and explain the internal structure of the earth and describe the formation and composition of earth's external features in terms of the rock cycle and plate tectonics and constructive and destructive forces

83996B10DFE601311C5068A86D17958E.description: Students, through the inquiry process, demonstrate knowledge of the composition, structures, processes and interactions of Earth's systems and other objects in space.

83992730DFE601311C4F68A86D17958E.description: create and use a basic classification scheme to identify plants and animals

8398E160DFE601311C4E68A86D17958E.description: investigate and explain the interdependent nature of populations and communities in the environment and describe how species in these populations adapt by evolving

83985720DFE601311C4C68A86D17958E.description: explain how organisms and systems of organisms obtain and use energy resources to maintain stable conditions (e.g., food webs, photosynthesis, respiration)

83980B30DFE601311C4B68A86D17958E.description: compare the structure and function of prokaryotic cells (bacteria) and eukaryotic cells (plant, animal, etc.) including the levels of organization of the structure and function, particularly with humans

8397BF80DFE601311C4A68A86D17958E.description: Students, through the inquiry process, demonstrate knowledge of characteristics, structures and function of living things, the process and diversity of life, and how living organisms interact with each other and their environment.

83977870DFE601311C4968A86D17958E.description: give examples and describe how energy is transferred and conserved (e.g. electric to light and heat [light bulb], chemical to mechanical [fuel to propulsion])

83972CA0DFE601311C4868A86D17958E.description: identify, build, describe, measure, and analyze mechanical systems (e.g., simple and complex compound machines) and describe the forces acting within those systems

8396C010DFE601311C4768A86D17958E.description: describe and explain the motion of an object in terms of its position, direction, & speed as well as the forces acting upon it

83965E50DFE601311C4668A86D17958E.description: model and explain the states of matter are dependent upon the quantity of energy present in the system and describe what will change and what will remain unchanged at the particulate level when matter experiences an external force or energy change

8364D390DFE601311C4468A86D17958E.description: examine, describe, compare and classify objects and substances based on common physical properties and simple chemical properties

83644CD0DFE601311C4268A86D17958E.description: Students, through the inquiry process, demonstrate knowledge of properties, forms, changes and interactions of physical and chemical systems.

83624AB0DFE601311C3B68A86D17958E.description: Students, through the inquiry process, demonstrate the ability to design, conduct, evaluate, and communicate results and reasonable conclusions of scientific investigations.

document.title: Montana K-12 Science Content Standards Framework

83555730DFE601311C3968A86D17958E.description: describe science as a human endeavor and an ongoing process

835513E0DFE601311C3868A86D17958E.description: describe how scientific inquiry has produced much knowledge about the world and a variety of contributions toward understanding events and phenomenon within the universe

8354D190DFE601311C3768A86D17958E.description: give historical examples of scientific and technological contributions to communities, cultures and societies, including Montana American Indian examples

83548CD0DFE601311C3668A86D17958E.description: Students understand historical developments in science and technology.

83544630DFE601311C3568A86D17958E.description: identify how the knowledge of science and technology influences the development of the Montana American Indian cultures

8353F610DFE601311C3468A86D17958E.description: use scientific knowledge to make inferences and propose solutions for simple environmental problems

8353B870DFE601311C3368A86D17958E.description: simulate scientific collaboration by sharing and communicating ideas to identify and describe problems

835375F0DFE601311C3268A86D17958E.description: describe a scientific or technological innovation that impacts communities, cultures, and societies

835332E0DFE601311C3168A86D17958E.description: describe and discuss examples of how people use science and technology

8352E610DFE601311C3068A86D17958E.description: Students, through the inquiry process, understand how scientific knowledge and technological developments impact communities, cultures and societies.

83528DF0DFE601311C2F68A86D17958E.description: identify technology and methods used for space exploration (e.g. star parties, space shuttles, telescopes)

83522100DFE601311C2E68A86D17958E.description: identify objects (e.g., moon, stars, meteors) in the sky and their patterns of movement and explain that light and heat comes from a star called the sun

8351DDF0DFE601311C2D68A86D17958E.description: identify seasons and explain the difference between weather and climate

83519FE0DFE601311C2C68A86D17958E.description: observe and describe the water cycle and the local weather and demonstrate how weather conditions are measured

83515E50DFE601311C2B68A86D17958E.description: investigate fossils and make inferences about life the plants, animals, and the environment at that time

83511F10DFE601311C2A68A86D17958E.description: describe and measure the physical properties of earth's basic materials (including soil, rocks, water and gases) and the resources they provide

8350DDD0DFE601311C2968A86D17958E.description: describe and give examples of earth's changing features

83509380DFE601311C2868A86D17958E.description: Students, through the inquiry process, demonstrate knowledge of the composition, structures, processes and interactions of Earth's systems and other objects in space.

83502AE0DFE601311C2768A86D17958E.description: create and use a classification system to group a variety of plants and animals according to their similarities and differences

834F8AD0DFE601311C2568A86D17958E.description: describe and use models that trace the life cycles of different plants and animals and discuss how they differ from species to species

834F4770DFE601311C2468A86D17958E.description: identify, measure, and describe basic requirements of energy and nutritional needs for an organism.

834F0940DFE601311C2368A86D17958E.description: identify that plants and animals have structures and systems that serve different functions for growth, survival, and reproduction

834EC940DFE601311C2268A86D17958E.description: Students, through the inquiry process, demonstrate knowledge of characteristics, structures and function of living things, the process and diversity of life, and how living organisms interact with each other and their environment.

834E7160DFE601311C2168A86D17958E.description: observe, measure and manipulate forms of energy: sound, light, heat, electrical, magnetic

834E35C0DFE601311C2068A86D17958E.description: identify, build, and describe mechanical systems and the forces acting within those systems

834CCA60DFE601311C1A68A86D17958E.description: Students, through the inquiry process, demonstrate knowledge of properties, forms, changes and interactions of physical and chemical systems.

834C8010DFE601311C1968A86D17958E.description: identify how observations of nature form an essential base of knowledge among the Montana American Indians

834C4110DFE601311C1868A86D17958E.description: identify a valid test in an investigation

834C0000DFE601311C1768A86D17958E.description: use models that illustrate simple concepts and compare those models to the actual phenomenon

829F5850DFE601311AFA68A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast a list of hypotheses to determine if they are testable.

829DF510DFE601311AF668A86D17958E.description: Distinguish the independent and dependent variables by examining a scientific experiment/investigation.

829CE580DFE601311AF368A86D17958E.description: Identify the various applications of scientific investigations (explore new phenomena, check on previous results, to test how well a hypothesis predicts, and to compare hypotheses

829C8B20DFE601311AF268A86D17958E.description: Generate a question, identify dependent and independent variables, formulate testable, multiple hypotheses, plan an investigation, predict its outcome, safely conduct the scientific investigations, and collect and anaylze the data.

829C23C0DFE601311AF168A86D17958E.description: Students, through the inquiry process, demonstrate the ability to design, conduct, evaluate, and communicate results and reasonable conclusions of scientific investigations.

document.title: Montana Common Core Standards for Mathematical Practices and Mathematics Content

7B4115C0DFE601310D9868A86D17958E.description: Design and use a simulation to generate frequencies for compound events.
comments: For example, use random digits as a simulation tool to approximate the answer to the question: If 40% of donors have type A blood, what is the probability that it will take at least 4 donors to find one with type A blood?

7B40D480DFE601310D9768A86D17958E.description: Represent sample spaces for compound events using methods such as organized lists, tables and tree diagrams. For an event described in everyday language (e.g., "rolling double sixes"), identify the outcomes in the sample space which compose the event.

7B409090DFE601310D9668A86D17958E.description: Understand that, just as with simple events, the probability of a compound event is the fraction of outcomes in the sample space for which the compound event occurs.

7B403A40DFE601310D9568A86D17958E.description: Find probabilities of compound events using organized lists, tables, tree diagrams, and simulation.

7B3FED90DFE601310D9468A86D17958E.description: Develop a probability model (which may not be uniform) by observing frequencies in data generated from a chance process.
comments: For example, find the approximate probability that a spinning penny will land heads up or that a tossed paper cup will land open-end down. Do the outcomes for the spinning penny appear to be equally likely based on the observed frequencies?

7B3F9C00DFE601310D9368A86D17958E.description: Develop a uniform probability model by assigning equal probability to all outcomes, and use the model to determine probabilities of events.
comments: For example, if a student is selected at random from a class, find the probability that Jane will be selected and the probability that a girl will be selected.

7B3F53A0DFE601310D9268A86D17958E.description: Develop a probability model and use it to find probabilities of events. Compare probabilities from a model to observed frequencies; if the agreement is not good, explain possible sources of the discrepancy.

7B3F0ED0DFE601310D9168A86D17958E.description: Approximate the probability of a chance event by collecting data on the chance process that produces it and observing its long-run relative frequency, and predict the approximate relative frequency given the probability.
comments: For example, when rolling a number cube 600 times, predict that a 3 or 6 would be rolled roughly 200 times, but probably not exactly 200 times.

7B3EB780DFE601310D9068A86D17958E.description: Understand that the probability of a chance event is a number between 0 and 1 that expresses the likelihood of the event occurring. Larger numbers indicate greater likelihood. A probability near 0 indicates an unlikely event, a probability around 1/2 indicates an event that is neither unlikely nor likely, and a probability near 1 indicates a likely event.

7B3E65F0DFE601310D8F68A86D17958E.description: Investigate chance processes and develop, use, and evaluate probability models.

comments: For example, decide whether the words in a chapter of a seventh-grade science book are generally longer than the words in a chapter of a fourth-grade science book.
7B3E0690DFE601310D8E68A86D17958E.description: Use measures of center and measures of variability for numerical data from random samples to draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.

comments: For example, the mean height of players on the basketball team is 10 cm greater than the mean height of players on the soccer team, about twice the variability (mean absolute deviation) on either team; on a dot plot, the separation between the two distributions of heights is noticeable.
7B3D9D10DFE601310D8D68A86D17958E.description: Informally assess the degree of visual overlap of two numerical data distributions with similar variabilities, measuring the difference between the centers by expressing it as a multiple of a measure of variability.

7B3D5B10DFE601310D8C68A86D17958E.description: Draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.

7B3D0F80DFE601310D8B68A86D17958E.description: Use data from a random sample to draw inferences about a population with an unknown characteristic of interest. Generate multiple samples (or simulated samples) of the same size to gauge the variation in estimates or predictions.
comments: For example, estimate the mean word length in a book by randomly sampling words from the book; predict the winner of a school election based on randomly sampled survey data. Gauge how far off the estimate or prediction might be.

7B3CC180DFE601310D8A68A86D17958E.description: Understand that statistics can be used to gain information about a population by examining a sample of the population; generalizations about a population from a sample are valid only if the sample is representative of that population. Understand that random sampling tends to produce representative samples and support valid inferences.

7B3C7DB0DFE601310D8968A86D17958E.description: Use random sampling to draw inferences about a population.

7B3BF070DFE601310D8768A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form px + q > r or px + q < r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Graph the solution set of the inequality and interpret it in the context of the problem.
comments: For example: As a salesperson, you are paid $50 per week plus $3 per sale. This week you want your pay to be at least $100. Write an inequality for the number of sales you need to make, and describe the solutions.
For example, the perimeter of a rectangle is 54 cm. Its length is 6 cm. What is its width?
7B3BA9B0DFE601310D8668A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems leading to equations of the form px + q = r and p(x + q) = r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Solve equations of these forms fluently. Compare an algebraic solution to an arithmetic solution, identifying the sequence of the operations used in each approach.

7B3B56B0DFE601310D8568A86D17958E.description: Use variables to represent quantities in a real-world or mathematical problem, and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems by reasoning about the quantities.

7B3AF920DFE601310D8468A86D17958E.description: Solve multi-step real-life and mathematical problems posed with positive and negative rational numbers in any form (whole numbers, fractions, and decimals), using tools strategically. Apply properties of operations to calculate with numbers in any form; convert between forms as appropriate; and assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies.
comments: For example: If a woman making $25 an hour gets a 10% raise, she will make an additional 1/10 of her salary an hour, or $2.50, for a new salary of $27.50. If you want to place a towel bar 9 3/4 inches long in the center of a door that is 27 1/2 inches wide, you will need to place the bar about 9 inches from each edge; this estimate can be used as a check on the exact computation.

7B3AAC70DFE601310D8368A86D17958E.description: Solve real-life and mathematical problems using numerical and algebraic expressions and equations.

7B3A60B0DFE601310D8268A86D17958E.description: Understand that rewriting an expression in different forms in a problem context can shed light on the problem and how the quantities in it are related.
comments: For example, a + 0.05a = 1.05a means that "increase by 5%" is the same as "multiply by 1.05."

7B3A1D70DFE601310D8168A86D17958E.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add, subtract, factor, and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients.

7B39D860DFE601310D8068A86D17958E.description: Use properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions.

7B3947E0DFE601310D7E68A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the four operations with rational numbers.
comments: Computations with rational numbers extend the rules for manipulating fractions to complex fractions.

7B390660DFE601310D7D68A86D17958E.description: Convert a rational number to a decimal using long division; know that the decimal form of a rational number terminates in 0s or eventually repeats.

7B38C4D0DFE601310D7C68A86D17958E.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide rational numbers.

7B387B00DFE601310D7B68A86D17958E.description: Understand that integers can be divided, provided that the divisor is not zero, and every quotient of integers (with non-zero divisor) is a rational number. If p and q are integers, then -(p/q) = (-p)/q = p/(-q). Interpret quotients of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.

7B381450DFE601310D7A68A86D17958E.description: Understand that multiplication is extended from fractions to rational numbers by requiring that operations continue to satisfy the properties of operations, particularly the distributive property, leading to products such as (-1)(-1) = 1 and the rules for multiplying signed numbers. Interpret products of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.

7B37C1D0DFE601310D7968A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division and of fractions to multiply and divide rational numbers.

7B376E60DFE601310D7868A86D17958E.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract rational numbers.

7B372320DFE601310D7768A86D17958E.description: Understand subtraction of rational numbers as adding the additive inverse, p - q = p + (-q). Show that the distance between two rational numbers on the number line is the absolute value of their difference, and apply this principle in real-world contexts.

7B36D7E0DFE601310D7668A86D17958E.description: Understand p + q as the number located a distance |q| from p, in the positive or negative direction depending on whether q is positive or negative. Show that a number and its opposite have a sum of 0 (are additive inverses). Interpret sums of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.

comments: For example, a hydrogen atom has 0 charge because its two constituents are oppositely charged.
7B369220DFE601310D7568A86D17958E.description: Describe situations in which opposite quantities combine to make 0.

7B364470DFE601310D7468A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of addition and subtraction to add and subtract rational numbers; represent addition and subtraction on a horizontal or vertical number line diagram.

7B35F120DFE601310D7368A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of operations with fractions to add, subtract, multiply, and divide rational numbers.

comments: Examples: simple interest, tax, markups and markdowns, gratuities and commissions, fees, percent increase and decrease, percent error.
7B3546C0DFE601310D7168A86D17958E.description: Use proportional relationships to solve multistep ratio and percent problems.

7B350510DFE601310D7068A86D17958E.description: Explain what a point (x, y) on the graph of a proportional relationship means in terms of the situation, with special attention to the points (0, 0) and (1, r) where r is the unit rate.

comments: For example, if total cost t is proportional to the number n of items purchased at a constant price p, the relationship between the total cost and the number of items can be expressed as t = pn.

7B3469B0DFE601310D6E68A86D17958E.description: Identify the constant of proportionality (unit rate) in tables, graphs, equations, diagrams, and verbal descriptions of proportional relationships.

7B342350DFE601310D6D68A86D17958E.description: Decide whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship, e.g., by testing for equivalent ratios in a table or graphing on a coordinate plane and observing whether the graph is a straight line through the origin.

7B33D5D0DFE601310D6C68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities.

comments: For example, if a person walks 1/2 mile in each 1/4 hour, compute the unit rate as the complex fraction <sup>1/2</sup>/<sub>1/4</sub> miles per hour, equivalently 2 miles per hour.
7B338F50DFE601310D6B68A86D17958E.description: Compute unit rates associated with ratios of fractions, including ratios of lengths, areas and other quantities measured in like or different units.

7B334A60DFE601310D6A68A86D17958E.description: Analyze proportional relationships and use them to solve real-world and mathematical problems.

7B329650DFE601310D6868A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area, volume and surface area of two- and three-dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes, and right prisms.

7B323CB0DFE601310D6768A86D17958E.description: Use facts about supplementary, complementary, vertical, and adjacent angles in a multi-step problem to write and solve simple equations for an unknown angle in a figure.

7B31F570DFE601310D6668A86D17958E.description: Know the formulas for the area and circumference of a circle and use them to solve problems; give an informal derivation of the relationship between the circumference and area of a circle.

7B31B240DFE601310D6568A86D17958E.description: Solve real-life and mathematical problems involving angle measure, area, surface area, and volume.

7B316CC0DFE601310D6468A86D17958E.description: Describe the two-dimensional figures that result from slicing three-dimensional figures, as in plane sections of right rectangular prisms and right rectangular pyramids.

7B3128E0DFE601310D6368A86D17958E.description: Draw (freehand, with ruler and protractor, and with technology) geometric shapes with given conditions. Focus on constructing triangles from three measures of angles or sides, noticing when the conditions determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle.

7B30E3D0DFE601310D6268A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving scale drawings of geometric figures, including computing actual lengths and areas from a scale drawing and reproducing a scale drawing at a different scale.

7B309AC0DFE601310D6168A86D17958E.description: Draw, construct, and describe geometrical figures and describe the relationships between them.

7B2FFEF0DFE601310D5F68A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

7B2FAA30DFE601310D5E68A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

7B2E4F50DFE601310D5A68A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

7B2DA1A0DFE601310D5868A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Montana Common Core Standards for Mathematical Practices and Mathematics Content

7A1FF9B0DFE601310C1868A86D17958E.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares, describe the shares using the words halves, fourths, and quarters, and use the phrases half of, fourth of, and quarter of. Describe the whole as two of, or four of the shares. Understand for these examples that decomposing into more equal shares creates smaller shares.

7A1FA380DFE601310C1768A86D17958E.description: Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles, and quarter-circles) or three-dimensional shapes (cubes, right rectangular prisms, right circular cones, and right circular cylinders) to create a composite shape, and compose new shapes from the composite shape.
comments: Students do not need to learn formal names such as "right rectangular prism."

7A1F5820DFE601310C1668A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between defining attributes (e.g., triangles are closed and three-sided) versus non-defining attributes (e.g., color, orientation, overall size); build and draw shapes to possess defining attributes.

7A1F17D0DFE601310C1568A86D17958E.description: Reason with shapes and their attributes.

7A1E8CB0DFE601310C1368A86D17958E.description: Organize, represent, and interpret data with up to three categories; ask and answer questions about the total number of data points, how many in each category, and how many more or less are in one category than in another.

7A1DE2D0DFE601310C1168A86D17958E.description: Tell and write time in hours and half-hours using analog and digital clocks.

7A1D5C30DFE601310C0F68A86D17958E.description: Express the length of an object as a whole number of length units, by laying multiple copies of a shorter object (the length unit) end to end; understand that the length measurement of an object is the number of same-size length units that span it with no gaps or overlaps.
comments: Limit to contexts where the object being measured is spanned by a whole number of length units with no gaps or overlaps.

7A1D17A0DFE601310C0E68A86D17958E.description: Order three objects by length; compare the lengths of two objects indirectly by using a third object.

7A1CBBC0DFE601310C0D68A86D17958E.description: Measure lengths indirectly and by iterating length units.

7A1C30D0DFE601310C0B68A86D17958E.description: Subtract multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 from multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 (positive or zero differences), using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.

7A1BF110DFE601310C0A68A86D17958E.description: Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less than the number, without having to count; explain the reasoning used.

7A1BAED0DFE601310C0968A86D17958E.description: Add within 100, including adding a two-digit number and a one-digit number, and adding a two-digit number and a multiple of 10, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used. Understand that in adding two-digit numbers, one adds tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose a ten.

7A1B6C50DFE601310C0868A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract.

7A1B20F0DFE601310C0768A86D17958E.description: Compare two two-digit numbers based on meanings of the tens and ones digits, recording the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, and <.

7A1AC440DFE601310C0668A86D17958E.description: The numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine tens (and 0 ones).

7A1A6FF0DFE601310C0568A86D17958E.description: The numbers from 11 to 19 are composed of a ten and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.

7A1A2410DFE601310C0468A86D17958E.description: 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a "ten."

7A19E3F0DFE601310C0368A86D17958E.description: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones. Understand the following as special cases:

7A195B70DFE601310C0168A86D17958E.description: Count to 120, starting at any number less than 120. In this range, read and write numerals and represent a number of objects with a written numeral.

7A18C070DFE601310BFF68A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

7A187040DFE601310BFE68A86D17958E.description: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers.
comments: For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of the equations 8 + ? = 11, 5 = - 3, 6 + 6 = .

7A182BB0DFE601310BFD68A86D17958E.description: Understand the meaning of the equal sign, and determine if equations involving addition and subtraction are true or false.
comments: For example, which of the following equations are true and which are false? 6 = 6, 7 = 8 - 1, 5 + 2 = 2 + 5, 4 + 1 = 5 + 2.

7A17E640DFE601310BFC68A86D17958E.description: Work with addition and subtraction equations.

7A179CF0DFE601310BFB68A86D17958E.description: Add and subtract within 20, demonstrating fluency for addition and subtraction within 10. Use strategies such as counting on; making ten (e.g., 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14); decomposing a number leading to a ten (e.g., 13 - 4 = 13 - 3 - 1 = 10 - 1 = 9); using the relationship between addition and subtraction (e.g., knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 - 8 = 4); and creating equivalent but easier or known sums (e.g., adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13).

7A174AC0DFE601310BFA68A86D17958E.description: Relate counting to addition and subtraction (e.g., by counting on 2 to add 2).

comments: For example, subtract 10 - 8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.
7A16CD10DFE601310BF868A86D17958E.description: Understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem.

7A168C00DFE601310BF768A86D17958E.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract.
comments: Students need not use formal terms for these properties.
To add 2 + 6 + 4, the second two numbers can be added to make a ten, so 2 + 6 + 4 = 2 + 10 = 12. (Associative property of addition.)
If 8 + 3 = 11 is known, then 3 + 8 = 11 is also known. (Commutative property of addition.)

7A164B70DFE601310BF668A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.

7A15FE20DFE601310BF568A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems that call for addition of three whole numbers whose sum is less than or equal to 20, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

7A15B2F0DFE601310BF468A86D17958E.description: Use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

7A154B30DFE601310BF368A86D17958E.description: Represent and solve problems involving addition and subtraction.

comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
7A14B6B0DFE601310BF168A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

7A146A70DFE601310BF068A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

7A131EE0DFE601310BEC68A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

7A127120DFE601310BEA68A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
